opportunities.title: Propose vulnerability identity key and lifecycle schema
opportunities.summary: ### Summary Inspect the committed Anchore JSON fixtures and propose a schema for tracking vulnerabilities over time. Specifically: what combination of fields uniquely identifies "the same vulnerability" across scans? Candidates to evaluate include CVE ID alone, CVE + package name, CVE + package name + version, and CVE + package + image. Write up the tradeoffs, pick a recommendation, and sketch the analytics DB table(s) needed to support first_seen / last_seen / fixed_at / ignored_at / cleared_at fields. **Tech notes:** The Anchore JSON schema is documented at the Anchore project site; worth skimming before diving into fixtures. The goal of this spike is a decision, not code — resist the urge to start implementing. ### Acceptance criteria - [ ] Written proposal (markdown doc in PR) covering identity key options, tradeoffs, and a recommendation - [ ] Proposed analytics DB schema with column types and rationale - [ ] At least one worked example from the fixtures showing how the identity key behaves across days - [ ] Reviewed and approved by Brandon and/or Matt before next ticket starts ## Bounty: $250 This issue has been selected for our paid contributor program. opportunities.title: [Bug bounty follow-up] tarsnap-recrypt can commit old-machine deletes while retaining a stale chunk directory
opportunities.summary: # [Bug bounty follow-up] tarsnap-recrypt can commit old-machine deletes while retaining a stale chunk directory I found a reproducible non-security crash-consistency gap in current `master` commit `0bf0b299fed91139044c81cc6fcdc5521c34d235` (`1.0.41-head`), after the fix for #746 / PR #747. At the end of `tarsnap-recrypt`, the old-machine delete transaction can be committed without any post-delete chunk directory being staged. An interruption or `unlink` failure immediately after that commit leaves a current sequence number but an old local directory which still claims that the deleted chunks exist. Disclosure: this issue was prepared with OpenAI Codex, an LLM, working on behalf of Sebastian Albrecht. The source path, commit state, subsequent deduplication decision, and fix control were independently rerun locally. Sebastian is available to discuss the report and answer technical questions. ## Cause The success tail in `recrypt/recrypt.c` performs: ```c storage_delete_end(SD); multitape_commit(ocachedir, omachinenum, oseqnum, 1, &storage_modified); unlink(odirpath); ``` Unlike a normal chunk deletion, this path never calls `chunks_delete_end` or `chunks_directory_write(..., ".tmp")`
opportunities.eligibilityReason: Payout evidence is below the bootstrap confidence threshold.

opportunities.title: [bounty $400] Implement ABNF-compliant email address parser with full §3.2–§4.4 coverage
opportunities.summary: `source.md` contains the complete RFC 5322 specification (Internet Message Format). We need a **fully conformant email address parser** in Python that implements the complete ABNF grammar from sections 3.2 through 3.4, plus obsolete syntax from §4.4. This parser must handle every edge case defined in the RFC — not just simple `user@domain` patterns, but the full complexity of quoted strings, comments, folding whitespace, group addresses, and domain literals. ## Background RFC 5322 defines email address syntax through a chain of ABNF productions that build on each other: ``` address = mailbox / group mailbox = name-addr / addr-spec name-addr = [display-name] angle-addr angle-addr = [CFWS] "<" addr-spec ">" [CFWS] addr-spec = local-part "@" domain local-part = dot-atom / quoted-string / obs-local-part domain = dot-atom / domain-literal / obs-domain ``` Each of these references further productions (CFWS, FWS, quoted-pair, dtext, etc.) that span multiple sections. **You must read `source.md` completely** to trace the full grammar dependency chain. ## Requirements ### 1. opportunities.title: parse_duration drops the days (d) unit
opportunities.summary: ## Bug `parse_duration` silently drops the **days** (`d`) unit. The README lists `d` as a supported unit, but the parser ignores it and returns a wrong (too-small) result instead of raising or counting it. ### Reproduction ```python from duration_utils import parse_duration parse_duration("1d") # -> 0 (expected 86400) parse_duration("2d4h") # -> 14400 (expected 187200) ``` ### Expected `d` should be counted as 86400 seconds, so `parse_duration("1d") == 86400` and `parse_duration("2d4h") == 187200`. ### Notes The `d` character is already accepted by the token regex, so malformed-input detection still passes — the value is just never added. A fix should add the `d` unit and cover it with tests. /bounty $50
